body:
What a topographical map reveals

A topographical map, commonly called a toposheet, presents detailed information about the physical and human-made features of a geographical area.

The Survey of India is India's national mapping organisation responsible for preparing and publishing topographical maps. Such maps have traditionally been prepared at scales including 1:25,000, 1:50,000 and 1:250,000.

At 1:50,000, every centimetre on the map represents 500 m on the ground. Relief is commonly represented through contours, while drainage, settlements, transport routes and vegetation are represented through conventional symbols.

Reading the marginal information

Marginal information consists of details provided around the main mapped area. It helps identify the map and interpret its contents.

  • Map title and geographical coverage.
  • Sheet number or reference.
  • Scale and north direction.
  • Contour interval and elevation units.
  • Conventional symbols and colours.
  • Survey, publication or revision dates where provided.

Survey and publication dates are especially important because roads, settlements, administrative boundaries and land use may change after a map is prepared.

Interpreting relief and drainage

Examine the elevations and arrangement of contours to identify high ground, low ground, hills, valleys and the general direction of slope.

Closely spaced contours indicate steep slopes, whereas widely spaced contours indicate gentle slopes when the contour interval is constant. River flow is normally towards decreasing elevation. Contour bends across stream valleys generally point upstream.

Interpreting settlement patterns

The distribution of buildings and villages may reveal different types of settlement patterns.

PatternAppearance on a map
CompactBuildings concentrated close together
DispersedBuildings scattered over a wider area
LinearBuildings arranged along a road, river or similar feature
CircularBuildings arranged around a central feature

Settlement patterns may be influenced by relief, water availability, transport routes, agricultural activities and other factors. A map can suggest relationships between these factors, but additional evidence may be needed to establish their causes.

Interpreting transport and land use

Roads, railway lines and bridges indicate connections between settlements and other locations. Forests, cultivated fields and built-up areas indicate different uses or characteristics of land.

Transport routes often respond to terrain. A road may follow a relatively gentle valley or avoid a steep hillside. However, engineering works such as bridges and tunnels may allow routes to cross difficult terrain.

A bridge symbol where a road crosses a river indicates a crossing. The road and river crossing alone, without an appropriate symbol or annotation, is not always sufficient to identify the nature of the crossing.

Integrated interpretation of an imaginary map

Consider a north-up topographical extract with a scale of 1:50,000 and a contour interval of 20 m.

A river crosses contours of 180 m, 160 m, 140 m and 120 m in that order from north to south. The contour bends point northwards. Village X lies west of the river, while Village Y lies east of the river. An east-west road connects the villages through a marked bridge. A forest area lies east of Village Y.

The map supports the following geographical conclusions:

  • The river flows southwards because its elevation decreases in that direction.
  • The contour bends point upstream towards the north.
  • Village Y lies east of Village X.
  • The road provides a connection between the villages across the river.
  • The forest is located farther east than Village Y.
  • The elevation difference between the highest and lowest labelled contours is 60 m.

These conclusions follow directly from the elevations, orientation and symbols provided. The map does not establish the exact population of the villages, the river's annual discharge or the forest's tree species unless additional information is supplied.

Gujarat example: a historical topographical sheet

A useful historical example is Survey of India topographical sheet 46 A/5, covering parts of the Banaskantha and Mahesana regions of northern Gujarat. The sheet represents an area surveyed during 1961-62 and was published in 1966.

Its scale is 1:50,000, equivalent to 1 cm representing 500 m. The geographical extent is 23°45′N to 24°N and 72°15′E to 72°30′E.

Interpretation of its contours and elevation information indicates that the northern and northeastern parts are generally higher than the western and southwestern parts. The broad direction of slope is therefore towards the southwest.

This example demonstrates how contours, elevation values and drainage information can be used together to understand the general relief of a region.

The sheet is a historical representation of conditions surveyed in 1961-62. Its settlement, drainage, land-use and transport information should not automatically be treated as a description of present-day conditions.

Distinguishing observation from inference

Direct observations are facts explicitly represented on a map, such as a marked road, a labelled elevation, a river or a forest boundary.

Inferences are conclusions drawn from those observations. For example, a series of decreasing contour elevations supports an inference about the direction of slope. A concentration of buildings along a road supports the identification of a linear settlement.

Good map interpretation relies on sufficient geographical evidence rather than assuming that every apparent relationship establishes a cause.

Prelims focus

  • The Survey of India prepares topographical maps of India.
  • At 1:50,000, 1 cm represents 500 m.
  • Marginal information includes scale, geographical coverage and contour interval.
  • A linear settlement is arranged along an elongated feature such as a road or river.
  • Relief and drainage should be interpreted together.
  • Trap: A historical map does not necessarily represent current ground conditions.

[References: NCERT, Practical Work in Geography, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 5, Topographical Maps, pp. 49-53 and 60-64; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Standard 11, 2020 reprint, Chapter 17, Topographical Sheets, pp. 124-131, particularly the interpretation of historical sheet 46 A/5 on p. 129, consulted 26 November 2026.]
